questions.prompt: A Task RAII wrapper holds std::coroutine_handle<promise_type> h and calls if (h) h.destroy(); in ~Task(). What happens if promise_type::final_suspend() returns std::suspend_never?
options: h.destroy() safely releases any remaining promise fields
When the coroutine finishes, its frame self-destructs before ~Task() runs, causing double destruction / use-after-free in ~Task()
Compilation fails unless final_suspend() returns std::suspend_always
The coroutine restarts from initial_suspend()
questions.explanation: Under [dcl.fct.def.coroutine], if a coroutine does not suspend at final_suspend(), execution flows off the end and automatically destroys the coroutine state. Any Task handle still pointing to that frame now dangles, so checking h.done() or calling h.destroy() in ~Task() is undefined behavior.

questions.prompt: Inside a coroutine body, how does the compiler translate co_yield expr;?
options: Into co_await promise.yield_value(expr);
Into promise.return_value(expr);
Into co_await expr; bypassing the promise
Into a thread yield call std::this_thread::yield()
questions.explanation: Per [expr.yield], co_yield expr is defined to be equivalent to co_await p.yield_value(expr), where p is the coroutine's promise object.

questions.prompt: Assuming Task starts lazily (initial_suspend() returns std::suspend_always), what happens when t.handle.resume() executes below?
options: msg was copied into the coroutine frame automatically, so msg.size() returns 5
Compilation fails because lambdas cannot be coroutines
Undefined behavior: the temporary lambda closure dies at the semicolon while t is suspended, so msg inside the coroutine reads a dangling closure this
HALO automatically extends the lambda closure lifetime to match t
questions.explanation: A coroutine lambda's captures reside in the closure object (*this), not in the coroutine's parameter list. Calling (...)() stores only the closure's this pointer inside the coroutine frame; when the temporary closure is destroyed at the semicolon, resuming t later dereferences a dangling this pointer.

questions.prompt: Why does make_task(std::string("transient")) exhibit undefined behavior when resumed after its initial suspension point?
options: std::string_view cannot be copied into a coroutine frame
co_await std::suspend_always{} clears all parameters
std::string temporaries cannot convert to std::string_view in coroutines
The coroutine frame stores a copy of sv (a pointer+length view), while the temporary std::string is destroyed at the semicolon before t.handle.resume() runs
questions.explanation: Coroutine parameters are copied/moved into the frame according to their declared parameter types. Because sv is a non-owning std::string_view (just like const std::string&), it does not extend or copy the backing std::string temporary, which dies at the end of the full-expression creating t.

questions.prompt: In void await_suspend(std::coroutine_handle<> h), the awaiter pushes h into a lock-free queue watched by another thread, and then reads this->result on the next line of await_suspend. Why is this a race / use-after-free?
options: await_suspend cannot accept a type-erased std::coroutine_handle<>

The coroutine is already suspended before await_suspend begins ([expr.await]), so the worker thread can resume and destroy the coroutine (and the awaited temporary awaiter) before await_suspend finishes
await_suspend automatically holds an internal mutex on h
Only bool await_suspend permits multi-threaded resumption
questions.explanation: Under [expr.await], the coroutine saves state and suspends before await_suspend(h) is entered. Once h is published to another thread, that thread may immediately resume h, run past co_await, and destroy both h and any stack/member awaiter object before await_suspend returns.

questions.prompt: How does returning std::coroutine_handle<> from await_suspend prevent stack overflow across long chains of completed coroutines, and what handle stops the chain?
options: It pushes continuations onto a heap queue; nullptr stops the chain
It spawns a fresh thread for each continuation; std::coroutine_handle<>::from_address(nullptr) stops it
It performs symmetric transfer via a tail call to the returned handle's resume() without growing the stack; returning std::noop_coroutine() returns control to the caller
It runs await_resume() recursively and unwinds with exceptions
questions.explanation: Under [expr.await], if await_suspend returns a std::coroutine_handle<Z>, the compiler emits a tail transfer calling resume() on that handle without allocating another C++ stack frame. Returning std::noop_coroutine() invokes a no-op resumption that immediately returns control to whichever caller invoked resume().
